meaning: the god of the atmosphere and sky

phonemes.desc: Short i as in “bit”, followed by the retroflex dental n — tongue curled back.
The d is retroflex ḍ in careful speech; the final a is a light schwa, half-sounded.

pronunciation.approximation: “IN-druh” — the final vowel breathes rather than lands
pronunciation.note: One of the oldest named gods in any Indo-European language — the name appears already in the Rigveda’s first hymn.

domains.title: God of the Storm, the Vajra, King of the Gods
domains.subtitle: The Dragon-Slayer of the Rigveda
domains.lead: Indra is the king of the Vedic gods: the thunderbolt-bearer who slew the dragon Vritra and released the rivers, the drinker of soma who roars into battle, the thousand-eyed lord of the sky. Two hundred and fifty hymns of the Rigveda are addressed to him — more than to any other deity — making him the best-documented god of the ancient world.

cards.name: The Vajra
cards.desc: The thunderbolt forged from the bones of the sage Dadhichi — Indra’s irresistible weapon against the dragon.

cards.name: Slayer of Vritra
cards.desc: He split the dragon that held the waters captive, and the rivers ran free — the founding victory of cosmic order.

cards.name: Lord of Soma
cards.desc: The sacred draught that makes gods gods: Indra drinks the soma press before every battle.

cards.name: The Thousand-Eyed
cards.desc: His body bears a thousand eyes — the marks of the gods’ curse and his redemption; the sky’s innumerable lights.

mythology.lead: The Indra of the Rigveda is a storm in divine form: mighty, boisterous, sometimes embarrassed, always central. His one great myth — the combat with Vritra — is the Vedic creation story: the waters of life imprisoned by the dragon, the thunderbolt that splits the mountains, the rivers released. Everything else in his mythology is commentary on that victory.

myths.title: The Slaying of Vritra
myths.text: Vritra, the “Enveloper”, coiled about the world’s waters and held them fast in his mountain caves. Indra, armed with the vajra forged by Tvashtri from Dadhichi’s bones, struck the dragon on its flank; the waters burst free and flooded to the sea. ‘Like lowing cows the waters rushed’ — the oldest dragon-slaying in recorded literature, and the template for every one after it.

myths.title: The Drink of Soma
myths.text: Before the combat, Indra drinks three lakes of soma pressed by the priests; filled with the draught, his strength is irresistible and his belly vast. The hymns taunt and flatter him by turns — the Vedic poets knew their storm-god was vain, and loved him for it. Soma is both his fuel and his fee.

myths.title: The Intoxication Hymn
myths.text: The most human hymn in the Rigveda: Indra speaks in the first person, drunk on soma, boasting — ‘I will break the earth’s two halves apart, like a gourd I will break the two worlds’. The gods’ king, for one hymn, sounds like a warrior at the feast, and the poets let him.

myths.title: From King of Gods to Dethroned Elder
myths.text: In the later epics the balance shifts: Vishnu’s avatars take the great victories, and Indra becomes the anxious king who sins — the seducer of Ahalyā, the raider of Triparu, the god who must yield his throne’s preeminence. The Purāṇas preserve a dignity-muted Indra, still lord of the eastern quarter and of the storm, but no longer the cosmos’ protagonist.

lore.syncretism: In Buddhism Indra becomes Śakra, lord of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, subservient to the Buddha and guardian of the dharma — the storm-god converted into a devotee. In Jainism he is a class of heaven-rulers. Greek observers heard Zeus in him; modern comparative philology confirmed the kinship: Indra and Zeus descend from the same Proto-Indo-European sky-father’s thunderbolt.
lore.culturalLegacy: He is embedded in the oldest Indo-European poetry extant — every study of dragon-slaying, thunder-gods, or soma/haoma ritual begins with him. The word ‘Indra’ entered Southeast Asian royal names (Indravarman, Indrapura) carried by Hindu expansion; and the Vajra passed east into Tibetan Buddhism as the thunderbolt-sceptre of the vajrayāna itself.
lore.extendedMeditation: Indra: a name with no diacritics because it never needed any — the retroflex consonants of the Vedic hymns sit quietly inside plain letters, as they have since the first singer pressed soma. To restore him in ASCII is to hand the thunderbolt back to the oldest god who still answers to the spelling a schoolchild would guess.
lore.archaeology: No Indra temples survive in India — the Vedic cult was fire and libation, not image. But his name is carved across Southeast Asia: the seventh-century Sanskrit inscriptions of Cambodia invoke him as royal ancestor, and Borobudur’s reliefs show Śakra attending the Buddha.
lore.cult: The Vedic cult of Indra centred on the soma-pressing: the great ritual whose three daily pressings were the engine of the storm-god’s power. His festival, the Indra-dhvaja, raised his banner at the monsoon’s onset — the ritual ancestor of every monsoon festival in the subcontinent.
lore.iconography: The thunderbolt in the raised right hand, the bow in the left; four arms in later iconography adding the goad and the lotus; his mount the white elephant Airāvata, his skin golden like the storm-light. The thousand eyes mark his body across his skin like stars.
lore.reception: Comparative mythology made Indra its cornerstone: the Vritra-combat mapped onto Thor’s, Zeus’, and Marduk’s victories established the field’s methods. In modern India, Indra survives in the monsoon’s personification, in the army’s missile named for his bolt, and in the unbroken recitation of the Rigveda itself — the oldest worship still vocally performed on earth.
